11   TAHOE REGIONAL PLANNING         No.  2:20-cv-00945-TLN-KJN           
    AGENCY,                                                              
12                                   ORDER                                
                 Plaintiff,                                              
13                                                                        
         v.                                                              
14                                                                        
    MOUNTAIN ADDICTION LLC and                                           
15   JUSTIN SHEAF,                                                        
16                Defendants.                                             
17                                                                        
18       This matter is before the Court on Plaintiff Tahoe Regional Planning Agency’s 
19  (“Plaintiff”) Motion to Strike or Dismiss the crossclaim filed by Defendants Mountain Addiction 
20  LLC and Justin Sheaf (collectively, “Defendants”) against third-party Defendant California Tahoe 
21  Conservancy (“CTC”).  (ECF No. 10.)  Defendants opposed the motion.  (ECF No. 13.)  Plaintiff 
22  replied.  (ECF No. 14.)                                               
23       Also before the Court is CTC’s motion to dismiss.  (ECF No. 17.)  Defendants filed an 
24  opposition.  (ECF No. 22.)  CTC filed a reply.  (ECF No. 23.)         
25       For reasons set forth below, the Court GRANTS Plaintiff’s motion (ECF No. 10) and 
26  DENIES CTC’s motion (ECF No. 17) as moot.                             
27  ///                                                                   
28  ///                                                                   
1       I.   FACTUAL AND PROCEDURAL BACKGROUND                           
2       Plaintiff alleges Defendants own property adjacent to over 500 acres of land owned by the 
3  State of California and managed by CTC (“CTC property”) in the Tahoe Region.  (ECF No. 1 at 
4  5.)  Plaintiff further alleges Defendants access federal public lands for winter activities, such as 
5  snowmobiling, by crossing CTC property.  (Id.)  Plaintiff alleges it received information from 
6  CTC in January 2020 that CTC property had been damaged behind Defendants’ property.  (Id.)  
7  Plaintiff inspected CTC property and found that at least 35 live trees had been cut, creating a 
8  snow trail from Defendants’ property.  (Id.)  Of the trees felled, five trees had a diameter-at-breast 
9  height (“dbh”) greater than 14.  (Id. at 5–6.)                        
10       On May 8, 2020, Plaintiff filed a complaint against Defendants, seeking civil penalties for 
11  multiple violations of the Tahoe Regional Planning Agency Compact and Code (“TRPA Code”) 
12  based on the tree cutting.  (See generally id.)  The TRPA Code specifies that removal of live trees 
13  having a dbh of greater than 14 requires a TRPA permit.  (Id. at 4.)  Plaintiff alleges Defendants 
14  cut down trees without a required permit to facilitate their access to public lands for snow cat and 
15  snowmobile use.  (Id. at 6–7.)                                        
16       On September 17, 2020, Defendants filed an answer and also brought a crossclaim against 
17  CTC, a third party to the action.  (ECF No. 8.)  Plaintiff filed the instant motion to strike or 
18  dismiss the crossclaim on October 8, 2020.  (ECF No. 10.)  Defendants filed an amended 
19  crossclaim (ECF No. 12) and opposition to Plaintiff’s motion (ECF No. 13) on October 29, 2020.  
20  In their amended crossclaim, which is substantially similar to the original crossclaim, Defendants 
21  allege CTC notified Plaintiff of the tree cutting in order to deprive Defendants of the use of CTC 
22  property.  (ECF No. 12 at 5.)  Defendants also claim CTC constructed a fence between 
23  Defendants’ property and CTC property to prevent Defendants’ access, while CTC did not 
24  construct a similar fence between CTC property and the ten other neighboring properties.  (Id.)  
25  Defendants request a judicial declaration that, as members of the general public, they have the 
26  right to utilize CTC property for summer and winter recreational activities.  (Id. at 7.)  Plaintiff 
27  filed a reply on November 4, 2020.  (ECF No. 14.)                     
28  ///                                                                   
1       II.  STANDARD OF LAW                                             
2       Under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure (“Rule”) 14, “a defending party may, as third-party 
3  plaintiff, serve a summons and complaint on a nonparty who is or may be liable to it for all or part 
4  of the claim against it.”  Fed. R. Civ. P. 14(a)(1).  The decision whether to implead a third-party 
5  defendant is addressed to the sound discretion of the trial court.  Southwest Adm’rs., Inc. v. 
6  Rozay’s Transfer, 791 F.2d 769, 777 (9th Cir. 1986).  “The crucial characteristic of a Rule 
7  14 claim is that defendant is attempting to transfer to the third-party defendant the liability 
8  asserted against him by the original plaintiff.”  Stewart v. Am. Int’l Oil & Gas Co., 845 F.2d 196, 
9  200 (9th Cir. 1988).  It is not sufficient that a third-party claim is related or arises out of the same 
10  set of facts.  U.S. v. One 1977 Mercedes Benz, 708 F.2d 444, 452 (9th Cir. 1983), cert. 
11  denied, 464 U.S. 1071 (1984).                                         
12       III.  ANALYSIS                                                   
13       Plaintiff moves to strike Defendants’ crossclaim against CTC under Rule 14 because the 
14  crossclaim does not allege CTC is liable for Defendants’ alleged tree-cutting violations.1 (ECF 
15  No. 10 at 3–4.)  In opposition, Defendants vaguely argue CTC’s liability depends on whether 
16  Defendants are found to have cut down the trees.  (ECF No. 13 at 4.)   
17       “[A] third-party claim may be asserted only when the third party’s liability is in some way 
18  dependent on the outcome of the main claim and the third party’s liability is secondary or 
19  derivative.”  One 1977 Mercedes Benz, 708 F.2d at 452; see also Stewart, 845 F.2d at 199–200.  
20  In the instant action, Plaintiff is suing Defendants for cutting down trees without a required 
21  permit in violation of the TRPA Code.  (ECF No. 1 at 7–8.)  In contrast, Defendants’ crossclaim 
22  seeks a judicial declaration of their right as members of the general public to use CTC property 
23  for recreational activities such as snowmobiling.  (ECF No. 12 at 7.)  Defendants have not shown 
24  their right to access CTC property is at all relevant to Plaintiff’s enforcement claim about cutting 
25  trees.  Defendants do not allege that they — or any other member of the general public — had a 
26                                                                        

27  1    Plaintiff also moves to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(1) and Rule 12(b)(6).  (ECF No. 10 at 9–
   12.)  Because the Court strikes the crossclaim under Rule 14(a)(4), the Court need not and does 
28  not address Plaintiff’s remaining arguments.                          
1  |  right to cut down trees on CTC property without a permit.  In any event, Defendants fail to 
2  |  explain how CTC is liable for Plaintiff's claim.  Defendants seek declaratory relief about 
3 || accessing CTC property for recreational use, not any payment or indemnification of civil 
4 |  penalties for the alleged tree cutting.  Because Defendants have not shown CTC “is or may be 
5  |  liable to [them] for all or part of the claim against [them],” Defendants’ crossclaim against CTC 1s 
6  |  improper and will be stricken.  See Fed. R. Civ. P. 14(a). 
7          IV.    CONCLUSION 
8          Based on the foregoing, the Court GRANTS Plaintiff's Motion to Strike (ECF No. 10), 
9  |  STRIKES Defendants’ crossclaim against CTC, and DISMISSES CTC from the action.  Further, 
10  | the Court DENIES CTC’s Motion to Dismiss (ECF No. 17) as moot. 
11          IT IS SO ORDERED.

21  Conservancy (“CTC”).  (ECF No. 10.)  Defendants opposed the motion.  (ECF No. 13.)  Plaintiff 
22  replied.  (ECF No. 14.)                                               
23       Also before the Court is CTC’s motion to dismiss.  (ECF No. 17.)  Defendants filed an 
24  opposition.  (ECF No. 22.)  CTC filed a reply.  (ECF No. 23.)         
25       For reasons set forth below, the Court GRANTS Plaintiff’s motion (ECF No. 10) and 
26  DENIES CTC’s motion (ECF No. 17) as moot.                             
27  ///                                                                   
28  ///                                                                   
1       I.   FACTUAL AND PROCEDURAL BACKGROUND                           
2       Plaintiff alleges Defendants own property adjacent to over 500 acres of land owned by the 
3  State of California and managed by CTC (“CTC property”) in the Tahoe Region.  (ECF No. 1 at 
4  5.)  Plaintiff further alleges Defendants access federal public lands for winter activities, such as 
5  snowmobiling, by crossing CTC property.  (Id.)  Plaintiff alleges it received information from 
6  CTC in January 2020 that CTC property had been damaged behind Defendants’ property.  (Id.)  
7  Plaintiff inspected CTC property and found that at least 35 live trees had been cut, creating a 
8  snow trail from Defendants’ property.  (Id.)  Of the trees felled, five trees had a diameter-at-breast 
9  height (“dbh”) greater than 14.  (Id. at 5–6.)                        
10       On May 8, 2020, Plaintiff filed a complaint against Defendants, seeking civil penalties for 
11  multiple violations of the Tahoe Regional Planning Agency Compact and Code (“TRPA Code”) 
12  based on the tree cutting.  (See generally id.)  The TRPA Code specifies that removal of live trees 
13  having a dbh of greater than 14 requires a TRPA permit.  (Id. at 4.)  Plaintiff alleges Defendants 
14  cut down trees without a required permit to facilitate their access to public lands for snow cat and 
15  snowmobile use.  (Id. at 6–7.)                                        
16       On September 17, 2020, Defendants filed an answer and also brought a crossclaim against 
17  CTC, a third party to the action.  (ECF No. 8.)  Plaintiff filed the instant motion to strike or 
18  dismiss the crossclaim on October 8, 2020.  (ECF No. 10.)  Defendants filed an amended 
19  crossclaim (ECF No. 12) and opposition to Plaintiff’s motion (ECF No. 13) on October 29, 2020.  
20  In their amended crossclaim, which is substantially similar to the original crossclaim, Defendants 
21  allege CTC notified Plaintiff of the tree cutting in order to deprive Defendants of the use of CTC 
22  property.  (ECF No. 12 at 5.)  Defendants also claim CTC constructed a fence between 
23  Defendants’ property and CTC property to prevent Defendants’ access, while CTC did not 
24  construct a similar fence between CTC property and the ten other neighboring properties.  (Id.)  
25  Defendants request a judicial declaration that, as members of the general public, they have the 
26  right to utilize CTC property for summer and winter recreational activities.  (Id. at 7.)  Plaintiff 
27  filed a reply on November 4, 2020.  (ECF No. 14.)                     
28  ///                                                                   
1       II.  STANDARD OF LAW                                             
2       Under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure (“Rule”) 14, “a defending party may, as third-party 
3  plaintiff, serve a summons and complaint on a nonparty who is or may be liable to it for all or part 
4  of the claim against it.”  Fed. R. Civ. P. 14(a)(1).  The decision whether to implead a third-party 
5  defendant is addressed to the sound discretion of the trial court.  Southwest Adm’rs., Inc. v. 
6  Rozay’s Transfer,
791 F.2d 769, 777
 (9th Cir. 1986).  “The crucial characteristic of a Rule 
7  14 claim is that defendant is attempting to transfer to the third-party defendant the liability 
8  asserted against him by the original plaintiff.”  Stewart v. Am. Int’l Oil & Gas Co.,
845 F.2d 196
, 
9  200 (9th Cir. 1988).  It is not sufficient that a third-party claim is related or arises out of the same 
10  set of facts.  U.S. v. One 1977 Mercedes Benz,
708 F.2d 444, 452
 (9th Cir. 1983), cert. 
11  denied,
464 U.S. 1071
 (1984).                                         
12       III.  ANALYSIS                                                   
13       Plaintiff moves to strike Defendants’ crossclaim against CTC under Rule 14 because the 
14  crossclaim does not allege CTC is liable for Defendants’ alleged tree-cutting violations.1 (ECF 
15  No. 10 at 3–4.)  In opposition, Defendants vaguely argue CTC’s liability depends on whether 
16  Defendants are found to have cut down the trees.  (ECF No. 13 at 4.)   
17       “[A] third-party claim may be asserted only when the third party’s liability is in some way 
18  dependent on the outcome of the main claim and the third party’s liability is secondary or 
19  derivative.”  One 1977 Mercedes Benz,
708 F.2d at 452
; see also Stewart, 845 F.2d at 199–200.  
20  In the instant action, Plaintiff is suing Defendants for cutting down trees without a required 
21  permit in violation of the TRPA Code.  (ECF No. 1 at 7–8.)  In contrast, Defendants’ crossclaim 
22  seeks a judicial declaration of their right as members of the general public to use CTC property 
23  for recreational activities such as snowmobiling.  (ECF No. 12 at 7.)  Defendants have not shown 
24  their right to access CTC property is at all relevant to Plaintiff’s enforcement claim about cutting 
25  trees.  Defendants do not allege that they — or any other member of the general public — had a 
26                                                                        

27  1    Plaintiff also moves to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(1) and Rule 12(b)(6).  (ECF No. 10 at 9–
   12.)  Because the Court strikes the crossclaim under Rule 14(a)(4), the Court need not and does 
28  not address Plaintiff’s remaining arguments.                          
1  |  right to cut down trees on CTC property without a permit.  In any event, Defendants fail to 
2  |  explain how CTC is liable for Plaintiff's claim.  Defendants seek declaratory relief about 
3 || accessing CTC property for recreational use, not any payment or indemnification of civil 
4 |  penalties for the alleged tree cutting.  Because Defendants have not shown CTC “is or may be 
5  |  liable to [them] for all or part of the claim against [them],” Defendants’ crossclaim against CTC 1s 
6  |  improper and will be stricken.  See Fed. R. Civ. P. 14(a). 
7          IV.    CONCLUSION 
8          Based on the foregoing, the Court GRANTS Plaintiff's Motion to Strike (ECF No. 10), 
9  |  STRIKES Defendants’ crossclaim against CTC, and DISMISSES CTC from the action.  Further, 
10  | the Court DENIES CTC’s Motion to Dismiss (ECF No. 17) as moot. 
11          IT IS SO ORDERED.
